title: The Basics Abandonment Problem
author: Scott D. Clary
summary: Kobe Bryant's practice of spending 45 minutes at 3:30 a.m. doing basic pivot moves and fundamental ball-handling drills illustrates a critical principle: excellence is built on relentless mastery of fundamentals. When asked why the world's best basketball player practiced such basic drills, Kobe replied, 'Because I never get bored with the basics.' The Basics Abandonment Problem describes how people and organizations often move past fundamentals before achieving true mastery, seeking novelty or advanced techniques prematurely. This applies across professions and personal development: sustained excellence requires returning repeatedly to core practices.
points: The world's best performers maintain obsessive focus on fundamentals and basic execution
Most people and organizations abandon basics prematurely in pursuit of novelty or advanced techniques
Boredom with fundamentals is often a sign of inadequate mastery, not expertise
Excellence is sustained through repetition and practice of core skills, not through constant advancement to new methods
The discipline to never get bored with basics separates sustained high performers from others
quotes: Kobe smiled: 'Why do you think I'm the best player in the world? Because I never get bored with the basics.' For 45 minutes, he sat there in disbelief. The best basketball player on the planet was doing footwork drills. Basic pivot moves. Fundamental ball-handling.
I call this the Basics Abandonment Problem: [the tendency to abandon fundamentals before achieving mastery]
No behind-the-back passes. No fancy fadeaways. No highlight-reel moves. Just the boring fundamentals. Executed with obsessive focus and maximum effort.
That line hit me hard: 'Because I never get bored with the basics.” Archived from Scott D. Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
